Charlie Parker was an American jazz saxophonist and composer whose rapid harmonic innovations and technical brilliance revolutionized jazz and defined the bebop style.

He was an alto saxophonist who pioneered bebop, a revolutionary style featuring fast tempos, complex harmonies, and horn-line improvisation that displaced the big-band swing era. Parker became famous for his quicksilver improvisations that navigated complex chord changes with unprecedented fluency, establishing the saxophone as a soloist's instrument.

He composed iconic bebop standards including "Billie's Bounce," "Ornithology," "Confirmation," and "Donna Lee," which became essential repertoire for generations of jazz musicians. Parker recorded prolifically with Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis, and his own ensembles, producing recordings that remain archetypal expressions of bebop's aesthetic.

His nickname was Bird, reflecting his fleet-footed, bird-like navigation of complex harmonic space. He became a cultural icon of the jazz rebel. Tragically, he died at age thirty-four in 1955, just as his influence was achieving its widest reach. His harmonic language influenced countless musicians, including Miles Davis, who played under his mentorship and absorbed his vocabulary before developing his own aesthetic. John Coltrane, a saxophonist of the next generation, built upon and transcended Parker's harmonic innovations.
